about: One table for the server, the app and the helper. The helper reads scripts with PowerShell's own parser; everything else here says how Rig's TypeScript reader sees a script, so the helper can match it. The vectors file holds examples of each rule, for scripts (`script`, `as`) and for whole steps (`cmd`).

Text: a script is refused when it is empty or only spaces, longer than `maxLength` characters (UTF-16 code units), or holds any character in `disguised` (hex ranges, inclusive). Case is folded for ASCII A-Z only, and only space, tab, CR and LF count as spaces; `disguised` holds the letters that fold into ASCII in .NET (U+017F, U+0130, U+0131, U+212A), so ASCII folding can't be tricked. CR LF and lone CR read as LF.

Commands: a command's name is folded. A name with \ or / is pathed: it must start with a `roots.known` entry and hold no `..`. The last part is the base; `exeSuffixes` are cut from its end, and then a base with a dot is a script file, refused. A base that is neither pathed nor had a suffix cut is looked up in `aliases` first. An entry with `exe` matches a base of that name whether pathed or not; one without `exe` matches only a plain name. With no entry: a read refuses it, a pathed program under `roots.unknown` is tier 2 with admin, any other pathed one is refused, and a plain Verb-Noun takes its tier from `verbs` (anything else is refused).

Arguments: an argument is a switch when written plain and it starts with - and a letter, -- and a letter, or / and a letter or ?. A parameter is - and a name, followed by a colon or the end of the word; text joined after the colon is its value. A comma between arguments only separates them (`a,b` is two arguments). An argument written as text with a variable or expression straight after it (`key=$x`) is that text, then a hidden argument. A variable, an expression, a double-quoted string with $ in it, or anything with a member or index after it is hidden. A redirection (`>`, `2>`, `*>` with its target) is not an argument, wherever it is written, as in PowerShell's own parser; a redirect to `$null` writes nothing, any other target is a write to that file. A script block's insides are read as more commands, and the block itself is not an argument.

Rules: a command's outcome is the first `when` rule that matches, else tier 0 if a `read` form matches, else the entry itself. `starts`: the first arguments equal these. `has`: some argument equals one. `prefix`: some argument starts with one, or, for an argument that starts with - or /, the part before any colon is at least two characters and one listed starts with it (PowerShell's short forms: -co fits -comp). `contains`: some argument contains one. `piped`: the command takes its input from the command before it in a pipeline. `after`: the tests look only at the values of the listed parameters (the next argument, or the text after a colon), with short forms fitting both ways. For a `never`, `refused` or tier 3 rule, a hidden argument counts as a match for starts, has and contains, and for prefix when the entry is `exe` or the rule has `after` (a program gets text, so a hidden argument could be anything; a cmdlet's hidden argument can only be a value).

Reads: a read form passes when the arguments begin with `starts`, include one of `has` when it is given, and every later argument that begins with - or / (the part before any colon) is in `params`, in `readParams`, or begins with one of `prefix`; short forms don't count here. `free` lets any written-out arguments follow, but no hidden one. `literal`: in a read every argument must be written out, and the command may not take pipeline input. `blocks`: every argument that isn't a switch must be a script block.

Targets: `targets` says what a command acts on. With `at`, the arguments at those positions (counting from 0, script blocks and the redirection `>` left out). Otherwise every argument that is not a parameter, plus the value after a parameter in `paths.literal` or one that `paths.literalPrefix` starts with (at least two characters), which is a literal target; the value after a parameter listed exactly in `values` is skipped. A target's place: fold, / as \, runs of \ as one, drop a leading `Microsoft.PowerShell.Core\`, `Registry::` or `FileSystem::`, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, HKEY_USERS and HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG as hkcu, hklm, hkcr, hku and hkcc, a hive followed by : or :\ as the hive and \, and no \ at the end. Its kind: registry (a hive, alone or with \), file (a letter, :\), drive (two or more letters and :), relative (has \ or :), or name.

Target checks, in every script: a target that isn't literal and holds a `paths.wildcards` character is refused (not for kind service); a place with a `..` part is refused. In a read, a `literal` command taking pipeline input is refused, and a kind outside `paths.readKinds` is refused. In a change, for `write`: a hidden target is refused, a relative one is refused, and at least one must be registry, file or drive. `content`: every target must be a file under one of `paths.readRoots` (`*` stands for one folder name; the place must be inside the root, and end with one of `ends` when given), with at least one target. `places`: in a change no target may end with one of `paths.programs`. A redirect target in a change is held to the same wildcard, `..`, program and hidden rules.

Programs a script wrote: in a change, a pathed command is refused when another command of tier 1 or more has a written-out argument with \ or / whose place is the program, its folder, or a folder inside or holding it, or when another such command has no `targets`, a hidden argument and isn't a read; a redirect target counts as such an argument. A plain `exe` command is refused when such a place ends with its name and one of `exeSuffixes`, or is `paths.system`.

Constructs: a script is refused for any find in `always`, a `static` member of a type literal not in `safeStatics` (written type::member or type.member, folded, without a leading system.), or any variable in `engine` (with any scope). In a read it is also refused for a type, a method call, a redirect or setting a member (`member-assign`). In a change, a type in `safeTypes` and a method in `safeMethods` are allowed, a redirect and setting a member are allowed with a reason, and any other type or method is refused. `pinned`: variables no script may assign, and no command may be given as an argument, with any scope or an env: or variable: drive in front. Finds: `unc` is any text whose \ and / read as \ holds \\ after a web address's scheme (two or more letters and :, not file:) is dropped; `provider` is text with alias:, function: or variable: at its start or after a \; `short-name` is a letter or digit, ~ and a digit.

Text rules: `neverText` and `protectText` are tested against the script and each touch after: fold; hkey_local_machine to hklm and hkey_current_user to hkcu; / to \; remove ` ' " + : and spaces; runs of \ become one. `neverText` refuses (reads are held only to entries with `applies` any); `protectText` makes a change tier 3. `adminText` makes a change need admin.

Steps: a step's touches are checked before its scripts: a registry key must start with HKCU or HKLM (as HKCU\, HKCU:\, HKEY_CURRENT_USER\ or Registry:: before any of those) and is stored as HKCU\ or HKLM\; a registry `value` must be a string; a file path must start with a letter and :\ with no `..` part and no short name; no touch may hold \\ or a wildcard. Each touch is held to `neverText` and `protectText`. A step's tier is the highest of its read, run and undo. `undo: null` is no undo. With no undo the step is tier 3 unless every touch is a registry key, file or service, there is at least one, and every write in `run` is covered: each place it writes (registry and file targets of a `write`, `places` or `content` command, service names, redirect targets) is a touch of the same kind or inside one. A write with no such place (a command without `targets`, a hidden or drive target) is never covered. A touch that no write in `run` reaches (either inside the other) adds an `unused-touch` reason.

constructs.unreadable: Rig can't read this script, so it won't run it
constructs.characters: This script uses curly quotes, long dashes or hidden characters that can disguise a command
constructs.too-long: This script is too long for Rig to check
constructs.empty: There is no script to check
constructs.dynamic: This script works out a command's name while it runs, so Rig can't tell what it would do
constructs.dot-source: This script loads another script into itself, which Rig can't check
constructs.obfuscated: A command's name is split up with backticks or quotes, which hides what it is
constructs.splat: This script passes arguments hidden in a variable, so Rig can't see them
constructs.keyword: Rig can't check scripts that define their own functions or use this keyword
constructs.provider-variable: This script reads or writes through a ${drive:path} variable, which Rig can't classify
constructs.dynamic-member: This script calls something on an object by a name worked out while it runs
constructs.stray: This script has a word Rig can't place
constructs.unc: This script reaches for another computer over the network, or has \\ or // in a path
constructs.type: This script uses .NET directly, and Rig can't tell what that would do
constructs.method: This script calls a method on an object, and Rig can't tell what that would do
constructs.redirect: This script writes its output to a file
constructs.path: This runs a program from outside C:\Windows\System32 and C:\Program Files
constructs.script-file: This runs another script or file that Rig can't read
constructs.unknown: Rig doesn't know this command, so it can't say what it would do
constructs.unknown-program: runs a program Rig doesn't know; Rig can't say what it changes
constructs.not-read: Rig only looks with the commands on its read list, and this isn't on it
constructs.not-literal: When Rig is only looking, paths have to be written out in full, not held in a variable
constructs.member-by-name: ForEach-Object is only allowed with a script block, because a bare name can call a method
constructs.touch: The list of what this changes has an entry Rig can't use; registry keys start with HKLM\ or HKCU\ and files with a drive letter
constructs.no-undo: There is no undo script, and Rig can't snapshot everything this touches
constructs.tainted: This can't be undone, and Rig has read text from outside in this chat, so it won't offer it
constructs.pinned: This script changes what decides which program or parameters a command really gets ($env:Path, $env:PSModulePath, $env:PATHEXT or $PSDefaultParameterValues), so Rig can't be sure what would run
constructs.provider: This script reaches commands or variables through the Alias:, Function: or Variable: drive, which can change what a command does
constructs.short-name: This script uses a short name such as PROGRA~1, which hides the real path
constructs.static: This script uses .NET directly, and Rig can't tell what that would do
constructs.static-variable: This script calls .NET through a type held in a variable, so Rig can't tell what it would do
constructs.member-assign: This script sets a property on an object directly, which Rig can't describe
constructs.engine: This script reaches into PowerShell itself, which can change what other commands do
constructs.wildcard: This names a place with *, ? or [ ], which can match places Rig would refuse; use -LiteralPath or write the name out
constructs.dots: This names a place with .. in it; write the full path instead
constructs.piped-read: When Rig is only looking, this command must name what it reads itself, not take it from the command before it
constructs.read-kind: When Rig is only looking, it reads only files and the registry, named in full
constructs.not-literal-change: This changes a place or value whose name is worked out while the script runs, so Rig can't check it; write it out in full
constructs.full-path: Rig only changes files and registry keys named by their full path, such as C:\... or HKCU:\...
constructs.read-place: Rig only reads files from Windows' logs, program folders, and the .log and .txt files apps keep in ProgramData and AppData
constructs.program-file: Rig doesn't copy, move or write program files, scripts or shortcuts
constructs.wrote-program: This runs a program from a place the same script changes, so it may not be the program Rig looked up
constructs.unused-touch: Rig expected each listed place to change, but the change script doesn't write there for

neverText.says: Rig never reads saved passwords, keys, sign-in stores or the Windows account database
Rig never reads the Windows sign-in settings, which can hold a saved password
Rig never shows saved Wi-Fi passwords
Rig never reads BitLocker recovery keys
Rig never downloads code and runs it, or unpacks hidden text into commands
Rig never changes what starts with Windows through the Run keys or the Startup folder; the startup apps fix does that safely
Rig never touches Image File Execution Options or SilentProcessExit, which can swap one program for another or start one when another closes
Rig never changes the Windows sign-in hooks
Rig never changes what runs when you sign in or open a command prompt
Rig never changes which program opens programs, scripts or Settings
Rig never turns on keeping sign-in passwords in memory (WDigest)
Rig never changes where Windows finds programs and their parts
Rig never changes which program a service runs
Rig never changes the hosts file
Rig never points this PC's proxy somewhere else
Rig never adds trusted root certificates
Rig never turns on ways into this PC from outside (Remote Desktop, WinRM, an SSH server)
Rig never changes its own files, log or guard

protectText.says: It changes User Account Control, which asks before apps get admin rights
It changes Microsoft Defender's settings or policy, which can turn protection off
It changes SmartScreen, Core isolation, Credential Guard or Safe Mode
It changes the Windows firewall's policy
It changes how one of Windows' security services starts (Defender, the firewall, Security Center, the event log or Windows Update)
